# Dates and text {#sec-m1-datas-strings}

In transport datasets, two kinds of column cause more work than all the others combined:
**dates** (in inconsistent formats) and **text** (names of municipalities, facilities,
commodities, addresses). This chapter handles both with `lubridate` and `stringr`.

```{r}
library(lubridate)
library(stringr)
```

## Dates with `lubridate`

### Reading

`lubridate`'s functions are named after the order of the components: `lubridate::dmy()` for
day-month-year, `lubridate::ymd()` for year-month-day, and so on. They tolerate different separators.
Brazilian data usually come as day/month/year.

```{r}
lubridate::dmy("28/09/2026")
lubridate::ymd("2026-09-28")
lubridate::dmy(c("28/09/2026", "05-10-2026", "3 nov 2026"))
lubridate::ymd_hms("2026-09-28 14:00:00")
```

Note that `R` always **stores** a date in the `YYYY-MM-DD` format (it is the `Date` object, a number
under the hood). The `28/09/2026` format only exists when **displaying** the date. To
display or export in the Brazilian format, use `format()`:

```{r}
d <- lubridate::ymd("2026-09-28")

format(d, "%d/%m/%Y")          # "28/09/2026"
format(d, "%d de %B de %Y")    # written out, in the system locale
```

The `%d/%m/%Y` pattern (day, month, 4-digit year) is the same vocabulary as `dmy()`/`ymd()`, only
for formatting instead of reading: `%d` day, `%m` month, `%Y` 4-digit year, `%y` 2-digit year.

```{r}
#| error: true
lubridate::dmy("2026-09-28")   # wrong order: returns NA with a warning
```

This is the most frequent error: reading a date column with the order swapped and getting `NA` in
part of the rows. Always check:

```{r}
datas_texto <- c("28/09/2026", "30/09/2026", "31/02/2026", "")
datas <- lubridate::dmy(datas_texto)
datas
sum(is.na(datas))    # how many failed?
datas_texto[is.na(datas)]  # which ones?
```

### Components and arithmetic

```{r}
d <- lubridate::ymd("2026-09-28")

lubridate::year(d); lubridate::month(d); lubridate::day(d)
lubridate::wday(d, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)   # depends on the system locale
lubridate::quarter(d)
lubridate::yday(d)          # day of the year

d + lubridate::days(15)
d + months(1)
d - lubridate::years(1)
lubridate::floor_date(d, "month")   # first day of the month
lubridate::ceiling_date(d, "month") - lubridate::days(1)  # last day of the month
```

### Intervals and durations

```{r}
inicio <- lubridate::ymd("2026-09-28")
fim    <- lubridate::ymd("2026-11-05")

fim - inicio                                  # difftime, in days
as.numeric(fim - inicio, units = "days")
lubridate::interval(inicio, fim) / months(1)             # in months
lubridate::time_length(lubridate::interval(inicio, fim), "weeks")   # in weeks
```

Typical application: trip duration from two timestamps (departure, `partida`, and arrival,
`chegada`, of three ships).

```{r}
viagens <- data.frame(
  navio   = c("Navio A", "Navio B", "Navio C"),
  partida = lubridate::ymd_hms(c("2026-03-01 08:30:00", "2026-03-02 22:10:00", "2026-03-04 06:00:00")),
  chegada = lubridate::ymd_hms(c("2026-03-04 17:45:00", "2026-03-07 09:05:00", "2026-03-05 23:30:00"))
)

viagens$horas <- as.numeric(difftime(viagens$chegada, viagens$partida, units = "hours"))
viagens$dia_semana <- lubridate::wday(viagens$partida, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
viagens
```

### Aggregating by period

```{r}
viagens$mes <- lubridate::floor_date(viagens$partida, "month")
aggregate(horas ~ mes, data = viagens, FUN = mean)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Time zone

`lubridate::ymd_hms()` assumes UTC by default. For Brazilian GPS or GTFS data, give
the time zone: `lubridate::ymd_hms(x, tz = "America/Sao_Paulo")`. Ignoring this produces three-hour errors in
travel-time calculations. It is a recurring problem when comparing data from different sources.
:::

## Text with `stringr`

All of the package's functions start with `str_`, take the text as their first argument and are
vectorised.

```{r}
cidades <- c("  Paranaguá ", "SÃO GONÇALO DO AMARANTE", "Rio Grande", "itajaí")

stringr::str_trim(cidades)                    # removes spaces at the ends
stringr::str_squish("Porto   de    Santos")   # also removes repeated spaces
stringr::str_to_upper(cidades)
stringr::str_to_lower(cidades)
stringr::str_to_title(stringr::str_to_lower(cidades))
stringr::str_length(cidades)
```

### Search, detect, replace

```{r}
instalacoes <- c("Terminal Portuário do Pecém", "Porto de Santos",
                 "IP4 Itacoatiara", "Terminais Fluviais do Brasil")

stringr::str_detect(instalacoes, "Terminal")          # TRUE/FALSE
stringr::str_subset(instalacoes, "Port")              # returns those that match
stringr::str_which(instalacoes, "Port")               # positions
stringr::str_replace(instalacoes, "Terminal", "Term.")    # first occurrence
stringr::str_replace_all(instalacoes, " ", "_")           # all of them
stringr::str_remove_all(instalacoes, "^IP\\d+ ")          # prefix such as "IP4 "
```

### Extract and split

```{r}
sh2 <- c("CT-Contêineres", "27-Combustíveis", "10-Cereais")

stringr::str_sub(sh2, 1, 2)                       # fixed position
stringr::str_split(sh2, "-", simplify = TRUE)     # splits into a matrix
stringr::str_extract(sh2, "^[A-Z0-9]+")           # before the hyphen
stringr::str_extract(sh2, "(?<=-).*$")            # after the hyphen
```

A very common case: splitting municipality and state from a single field.

```{r}
locais <- c("Paranaguá/PR", "Santos/SP", "São Luís/MA")

data.frame(
  municipio = stringr::str_extract(locais, "^[^/]+"),
  uf        = stringr::str_extract(locais, "[A-Z]{2}$")
)
```

### Regular expressions in a table

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `^` / `$` | start / end of the text | `^BR` matches "BR-116" |
| `\\d` | one digit | `BR-\\d{3}` matches "BR-116" |
| `\\s` | space | `\\s+` one or more spaces |
| `[A-Z]{2}` | two capital letters | state abbreviation |
| `.` | any character | `a.c` matches "abc" |
| `*` `+` `?` | 0+, 1+, 0 or 1 repetitions | `\\d+` a number |
| `(?<=x)` | *lookbehind*: after "x" | `(?<=-)\\d+` |
| `|` | or | `Porto|Terminal` |

In R, the backslash must be doubled inside a string: `"\\d"` is the digit.

```{r}
rodovias <- c("BR-116/PR", "BR 277", "PR-508", "br-153 km 45")

stringr::str_extract(rodovias, "\\d{3}")
stringr::str_detect(stringr::str_to_upper(rodovias), "^BR")
stringr::str_extract(rodovias, "(?i)km\\s*\\d+")
```

### Standardising to join datasets

The most important use of `stringr` in the course: preparing a join **key**. Municipality
names come with different accents, case and spacing in each dataset.

```{r}
padronizar <- function(x) {
  x |>
    stringr::str_squish() |>
    stringr::str_to_lower() |>
    stringi::stri_trans_general("Latin-ASCII") |>  # removes accents
    stringr::str_remove_all("[^a-z ]")                      # removes punctuation
}

base_a <- c("São Gonçalo do Amarante", "Paranaguá", " Rio  Grande ")
base_b <- c("SAO GONCALO DO AMARANTE", "PARANAGUA", "RIO GRANDE")

data.frame(
  base_a, base_b,
  igual_cru  = base_a == base_b,
  igual_pad  = padronizar(base_a) == padronizar(base_b)
)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Standardising municipality names solves most cases, but **not all**: there are
municipalities with the same name in different states (for example, *Bonito* exists in MS, PA, PE and BA).
Whenever possible, use the **7-digit IBGE code** as the key, and the name only for
human reading. We deal with this in @sec-m1-joins.
:::

### Building text

```{r}
uf <- "PR"; tku <- 8.33

stringr::str_c("Ligação com destino ", uf, ": ", tku, " bi TKU")
stringr::str_glue("Ligação com destino {uf}: {tku} bi TKU")
sprintf("Ligação com destino %s: %.2f bi TKU", uf, tku)
stringr::str_pad(c("1", "23", "456"), width = 3, pad = "0")   # codes with leading zeros
```

::: {.callout-note}
We use `stringi::stri_trans_general()` instead of `iconv(to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT")` because
`iconv`'s result varies between Windows, macOS and Linux. On Windows, it sometimes returns
`?` instead of the accented letter. `stringi` is already installed together with `stringr`.
:::

`str_pad()` solves a classic problem: municipality or census tract codes read
as numbers lose their leading zero. `str_pad(cod, 7, pad = "0")` restores them.
